video.title: How to Make $15k/M on FB Marketplace Selling This ONE Item

summary: Chris Koerner re-interviews Alex Nelson, 'the Shelf Dude' from Utah, who makes custom wooden shelving for storage totes and sells it exclusively through Facebook Marketplace. Alex charges about $40 per tote space, spends about $150 in materials on a $1,000 shelf, quit his job in May 2024 and reached about $15k/month net profit. Since then he has added digital plans, an eight-module course and an installer network on a 70/30 split, because shelving brings no repeat customers. They discuss Marketplace best practices: many free listings, price testing, boosting in competitive markets, and in-person visits that close 100% of the time.

speakers.name: Alex Nelson
speakers.description: 'The Shelf Dude', Utah-based builder of tote storage shelving

ideas.name: Custom tote garage shelving sold on Facebook Marketplace (The Shelf Dude)
ideas.one_liner: Build and install wooden shelving units that hold standard black-and-yellow storage totes, sold and closed via Facebook Marketplace listings and Messenger.
ideas.business_model: Per-job custom build and install, priced per tote space
ideas.customer: Homeowners in Utah Valley with garages full of stacked storage totes
ideas.problem: Stacked totes are hard and stressful to access; people pull their backs unstacking them
ideas.offer: Custom wood-and-wheels shelving structure sized to the customer's totes (totes not included), built and installed

pricing.notes: Price varies across listings ($25-$40 per space) to test demand; totes bought separately by customer.

acquisition_channels.details: Many Facebook Marketplace listings with before/after photos of stacked vs shelved totes; leads handled in Messenger; boosting tried with little success.

quote.text: all of your leads were coming from either Facebook Marketplace or from referrals from Facebook Marketplace, right? >> Correct
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

acquisition_channels.details: Instagram reels later built a following of organisers and installers.

ideas.delivery: Alex builds the shelves in a rented shop and delivers/installs on Saturdays (initially with a borrowed truck); in-person measuring visits close at 100%.
ideas.startup_cost: Low: tools, wood, borrowed truck; later a rented shop
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Quickly after first listing in late 2023; full-time by May 2024

acquisition.how: Marketplace listing creation can be scripted/AI-written but message handling and site visits are human; UK seller listing is inbound so legal.

onboarding.how: Measuring visits and photo review by a person.

uk_applicability.notes: Facebook Marketplace and tote shelving work in the UK; UK garages are smaller and fewer, and storage tote sizes differ (e.g. Really Useful Boxes), so design and pricing need changes.

risks: Non-recurring product: one shelf lasts forever

quotes.text: I make the shelving units for those black and yellow totes you can get at any of the big box stores
quotes.speaker: Alex Nelson

quotes.text: in our first video I was charging $40 per per tote per space and it's the same today
quotes.speaker: Alex Nelson

ideas.name: Shelf Dude installer network (lead referral with 70/30 split)
ideas.one_liner: Forward out-of-area leads to a network of independent installers who build shelves, with Alex keeping 30% of the job.
ideas.business_model: Lead referral revenue share (30%) plus paid 'Shelf Dude Pro' tier for listing/exclusivity
ideas.customer: Independent shelf builders/installers in other cities and countries
ideas.problem: Alex gets leads from Oshkosh, Florida, Australia he cannot serve; installers need leads
ideas.offer: Leads routed to installers; free tier for connection, paid Pro tier gives website listing, location, territory exclusivity, hat and shirt

acquisition_channels.details: Inbound leads from Alex's Instagram/Facebook following and website shelfdude.com forwarded to installers.

ideas.delivery: Installers build and install; Alex routes leads and lists installers on the website.
unit_economics_claims: 70/30 split: on a $1,000 shelf installer gets $700, Alex $300
Installer material cost ~ $150, ~80% margin for installer

acquisition.how: Inbound leads from content/website can be auto-routed by territory.

onboarding.how: Installer sign-up and listing can be self-serve.

support.how: Disputes between customers and installers need a human.

uk_applicability.notes: A referral network for home installers is legal in the UK; recruiting installers must be inbound or via cold email to limited companies only (PECR).

quotes.text: There's kind of a 7030 split. If you think of a $1,000 shelf, that's obviously 300. 700 of their 700
quotes.speaker: Alex Nelson

ideas.name: Digital shelf plans and 8-module course
ideas.one_liner: Sell downloadable PDF build plans and an eight-module course on building and selling tote shelves.
ideas.problem: People want to build the shelves themselves or start the same business
ideas.offer: PDF plans (now professionally redrawn by a hired plan maker) and an 8-module course covering building and Facebook selling

acquisition_channels.details: Sold via shelfdude.com to followers and enquirers.

ideas.delivery: Digital download; a contractor now draws new plans (e.g. the tote bed).

support.how: Questions answerable by an agent trained on the course.

uk_applicability.notes: Digital plans sell the same in the UK; metric dimensions would help.

quotes.text: I made the first plans that you could buy online just kind of digital download on my computer myself PDF Adobe
quotes.speaker: Alex Nelson

ideas.name: Annual garage spring-clean subscription for past customers
ideas.one_liner: Sell an annual garage cleaning/organisation service to the ~1,000 past shelf customers.
ideas.problem: Garages get cluttered again; shelf business has no repeat revenue

acquisition_channels.details: Email the customer database of every buyer and plan purchaser.

ideas.delivery: Labour by Alex, a friend, or hired help.

acquisition.how: Emailing existing customers who bought is soft opt-in friendly in UK if they were given an opt-out.

uk_applicability.notes: Works the same in the UK; email to existing customers allowed under PECR soft opt-in for similar services.

risks: Jobs vary a lot so pricing is hard

quotes.text: you get 10% of them to sign up for like annual spring cleaning services, right? 600 bucks, right? That could be 600 times 100 60,000
quotes.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.name: Monetise competitors as garage-cleanup referral partners
ideas.one_liner: Pay rival Marketplace shelf sellers $100 per garage-cleanup lead they refer.
ideas.problem: Competitors undercut on price; they get cleanup requests they won't do

acquisition_channels.details: Build a database of local Marketplace competitors and offer them $100 per referred lead.

acquisition.how: Contacting individual sellers via Messenger is unsolicited marketing to individuals/sole traders, not allowed in the UK under PECR without consent.

uk_applicability.notes: Concept works but cold-messaging sole-trader competitors on Facebook is restricted by PECR; would need inbound or limited-company targets.

quotes.text: Every lead you send me, I'll give you a hundred bucks." And you could have like this network of referral partners
quotes.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.name: Copy popular Pinterest/Etsy build plans and sell builds on Marketplace
ideas.one_liner: Find popular furniture/organisation designs on Pinterest, Etsy or plan sites and use the same Marketplace playbook to sell them built.
ideas.business_model: Product sales of locally built items
ideas.offer: Built versions of proven designs (coffee tables, tables, shelving)

acquisition_channels.details: Post pictures on Facebook Marketplace to test demand before scaling.

acquisition.how: Trend research and listing writing can be automated; Marketplace is inbound.

quotes.text: go to Pinterest or Etsy or a site that sells plans like this and like look at the number of comments or sort by most popular
quotes.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.name: Thrift/free-item flipping on Facebook Marketplace
ideas.one_liner: Pick up free or cheap items (home gyms, church pews, thrift store goods) and resell them.

acquisition_channels.details: Browse the Marketplace homepage and thrift stores (e.g. Deseret Industries) for underpriced items.

acquisition.how: Deal spotting can be scripted; listings AI-written.

uk_applicability.notes: Works in the UK with charity shops and Gumtree/Marketplace.

quotes.text: We got a free home gym. Okay. Well, you could sell that stuff. Go get it for free and then sell it
quotes.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.name: Tote storage bed
ideas.one_liner: Kids' bed frame with tote shelving underneath, sold as a variant of the shelf product with plans.
ideas.offer: Bed with tote shelves under it, plus plans

acquisition_channels.details: Video being prepared for release on social.

tactics.name: Spray-and-pray Marketplace listings
steps: Create many listings; each costs nothing without ads
Use ChatGPT to generate listing ideas and vary wording (change one word)
Vary price across listings ($25/$32/$40 per space) to test demand
Double down on the listing that works

quote.text: It doesn't cost you a thing to make a listing. So, make as many as you can. Use chat GPT to come up with ideas
quote.speaker: Alex Nelson

tactics.name: Boost listings in competitive markets
steps: Put ~$20 behind it as a boost when competitors crowd search
Higher visibility lets you hold price against undercutters

quote.text: the more competing listings there are, the more you're boosting uh can make a difference. It can put you at the top of the search results
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Before/after photo listings
steps: Photograph stacked messy totes vs organised shelf side by side
Let photos sell; video not needed early

tactics.name: Messenger qualification then in-person measure
steps: Ask customer to send pictures of their space to look expert
Offer to come measure; in-person visits close 100%

quote.text: what's your space look like? Send me pictures and kind of create that professionalism there and let them know that I'm the expert
quote.speaker: Alex Nelson

tactics.name: Paint the emotional picture
steps: Tell prospects how they will feel when the job is done
Anticipate emotional reactions (land clearing customers cry) and state it upfront

tactics.name: Turn a non-recurring product into recurring/leveraged revenue
steps: Route excess leads to installer network on 70/30 split
Paid Pro tier with territory exclusivity
Upsell organising/cleanup services to past customers

lessons.lesson: Listings are free, so volume testing of many listing variants is the cheapest validation.

quote.text: It doesn't cost you a thing to make a listing. So, make as many as you can
quote.speaker: Alex Nelson

lessons.lesson: In crowded Marketplace categories, small paid boosts can restore visibility and let you keep higher prices.

quote.text: Boosting also enables you to keep a higher price because more eyeballs equal higher price
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: A winning product can usually be replicated with a different product using the same distribution playbook.

quote.text: Oftentimes, in fact, usually in my experience, it can be replicated with a different product or service
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: Getting into the customer's space in person drives very high close rates for physical services.

quote.text: Hey, can you come measure for me? Sure. I always close them
quote.speaker: Alex Nelson

lessons.lesson: For a one-off product, add leverage: plans, courses, installer networks, and services to past customers.
Customer feedback on early listings (too expensive, other versions) tells you what to build next.

quote.text: If you get a lot of feedback saying, "Oh, this is too expensive." Or, "Hey, do you have this version?" Well, all those little details go into making a better version
quote.speaker: Alex Nelson

lessons.lesson: Price perception varies by customer; some say it's cheaper than expected, so test higher prices.

quote.text: I'm telling them the price and they say, "Oh, I I would have thought it'd be be more."
quote.speaker: Alex Nelson

lessons.lesson: Time-cost your craft: if hourly earnings are below a job's wage, speed up or change product.
You can monetise competitors by making them referral partners instead of fighting them.

evidence_quality.rationale: First-hand operator with consistent pricing, cost and split numbers; the $15k/month figure is from the earlier episode.
